pending_qa.q: Is Rahm Emanuel right to publicly attack the DSA as a threat to Democratic electability?
pending_qa.r: Hayes acknowledges a kernel of truth in Emanuel's concern — that a primary electorate can select candidates poorly optimized for a general election — but argues that publicly amplifying the issue in the Wall Street Journal is counterproductive. He says it raises the salience of problematic issues without dissuading DSA activists, pointing to the UK Labour Party as a cautionary example: picking 'high-profile fights with the left flank' on immigration and trans issues 'didn't work' because it kept those issues constantly in the press.

pending_qa.q: What tactical error has AIPAC made in Democratic primaries according to Chris Hayes?
pending_qa.r: Hayes argues that AIPAC has made 'an enormous tactical error' by relying on a strategy of 'attempting to trick voters as opposed to making their case.' He notes that AIPAC-backed spending has driven some of the most expensive primaries in history — citing the Jamal Bowman race, the Cori Bush-Wesley Bell race, and spending of at least $30 million in Michigan — and that the vast majority of their ads were not about Israel but instead tried to paint targeted candidates as insufficiently loyal.

pending_qa.q: How does Donald Trump's economic approach compare to progressive or socialist economic policies?
pending_qa.r: Hayes argues that Trump is 'the most antagonistic president to free markets' he has ever seen, describing him as 'fundamentally authoritarian, illiberal' and a believer in 'a personalist controlled economy.' He frames Trump as ideologically closer to pre-Adam Smith mercantilism than to any coherent market ideology, noting that Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations was itself 'written as a polemic against tariffs and mercantilism.' Hayes warns against Democrats calling Trump a socialist, saying it is 'a boner killer for everybody' and that Trump is 'in his own category — like a pre-Adam Smith monarch.'

pending_qa.q: What is the key risk of progressive primary wins not translating to general election success?
pending_qa.r: Hayes uses a basketball analogy: just as a player needs 'a completely delusional sense of their own ability' to reach the NBA, a candidate like Mamdani must believe in themselves to win — but 'everyone else should be pretty clear eyed' that there is 'a trade-off about where you are on the ideological spectrum.' He warns it is 'obviously a true thing' that a 'very motivated, disproportionately highly educated Democratic primary electorate' can select candidates 'too ideologically extreme to win generals,' citing Blake Masters, Mark Robinson, and Christine O'Donnell as examples from the Republican side.
